extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and advanced undergraduate/graduate students in analysis and geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and conditions for reducing certain definite and indefinite trigonometric integrals to simpler elementary integrals or known special functions, together with related theorems about surfaces of the second order and tangents of algebraic curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cosine-product expansion for integral reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Products of cosine factors may be expressed as sums/products of cosines of shifted arguments (e.g., 2 cos zx = cos(z+a)x + cos(z+2λ)x = 2 cos λx cos(z+λ)x etc.), enabling reduction of integrals involving products like (cos λx)^p (cos μx)^q ... to sums of simpler cosine factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the given identities repeatedly to expand products of cosines into sums with arguments shifted by multiples of the fundamental quantities (λ, μ, ...); differentiate with respect to parameters (z, etc.) to derive families of related integrals. Many particular definite and indefinite integrals follow from this general formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter positivity requirement (z > 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many derived integral formulae (particularly those produced by the cosine/sine expansions), the parameter z must be positive; in sine-integral formulae z must be positive and cannot be zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the reduction formulae and differentiations, ensure z>0 (and z ≠ 0 for certain sine integrals) to avoid invalid or singular cases; the text repeatedly states 'Here z must be positive' or 'z must be positive and cannot be zero.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation with respect to parameters to obtain related integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate the general integral representations with respect to parameters (z, p, m, n, etc.) to obtain new integrals involving extra polynomial or logarithmic factors (e.g., factors of x, powers, logs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manuscript shows multiple examples: differentiate a base integral identity in parameter z (or change parameter e.g. A→h−1) and differentiate to obtain integrals containing sin(...) or log(cos) factors and higher powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity beyond integer indices via analytic continuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although many preceding integrals are obtained under the supposition that m, n, etc., are integers, they are equally true for non-integer values; this follows immediately from formal series/operation formulas (analytic continuation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not restrict application only to integer exponents where the algebraic manipulations produce identities valid in general; the text explicitly notes that the identities hold 'whatever be these quantities.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbolic operators when closed forms impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: In many cases it is not practicable to represent values of integrals except by means of symbols of operation; multiple such symbols may be combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to express reduced integrals in operational-symbol notation (iterated differential operators, symbolic transforms) when explicit elementary expressions are cumbersome or unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction formulas for V_{m,n} (three alternative forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the class of integrals denoted V_{m,n}, three reduction forms are given: (1) relation reducing V_{m,n} to V_{m-1,n-?} with coefficients involving m, n, (2) alternate form useful when m reaches certain values, (3) third form reducing different index combos. The three formulas admit different reduction pathways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate form depending on parameter values; note failure cases: when m=0 the first form fails to reduce certain indices, and when m=2n−1 second and third coincide causing other failures. Identify which of V_{i,0} (i=0,−1, etc.) remain as elementary kernels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional reduction cases and final elemental integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: There are exceptional parameter values where particular reduction formulae fail (e.g., m=0, m=2n−1); however overall every V_{m,n} reduces to one of the elemental integrals V_{i,0} (specifically V_{i,0} with i in {−1,0,...}), leaving only V_{0,0} and V_{−1,0} (which reduce to known integrals involving logarithms or Spence's function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When performing reduction, track exceptional index values and switch to alternate reduction forms; the remaining base integrals are handled by substitutions that lead to integrals expressible via log-sine/log-cosine forms and Spence's L (dilogarithm) or the i-function described in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy for exponential/trigonometric-log integrals: substitution to Spence's L
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrals that appear exponential in form (or integrals like ∫ log z dz with z substitution leading to rational/exponential forms) can be transformed via substitutions (e.g., z = (1+t)/(1−t) or similar) so that they reduce to combinations of log terms and Spence's function L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the substitutions indicated (e.g., set z=(1+t)/(1−t), set u transforms) and use known integrals of log(1±u) and identities to write results in terms of log^2, products of logs, and Spence's L. The paper works through these reductions in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry and special values of the i_r function
rubrics_metrics.description: For the function i_r(a) = −∫_0^a log(sin x) dx (with sign chosen to make i_r positive), there are symmetry relations: i_r(a)+i_r(π−a)=i_r(π/2) and 2 i_r(π/2)=i_r(π); specifically i_r(π/2)= (π/2) log 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these symmetry relations to reduce the domain of computation (only need values up to π/2). The text gives expansions and special-case limits (e.g., at a→π/2 the series gives i_r(π/2)= (π/2) log 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Series expansions for i_r in cos powers and convergence remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: i_r has expansions in powers of cos x with coefficients A_n given recursively and asymptotic behavior for large n (An tends to expression involving log 2n), and expansions that are useful when x is small or near π/2 with convergence dependent on smallness of t (t = x^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To compute i_r numerically or in series form, use the provided recurrence for A_n and the series representation; beware slow convergence unless the expansion variable is small (choose appropriate expansion region).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of integrals via tangent-substitution / differentiation identity
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining tangents of algebraic curves: substitute y = m x + c into the curve equation and require that two roots coincide (double root) which is equivalent to equating the coefficient of first power terms to zero — effectively an operation identical with differentiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find the slope m of the tangent at (x',y') translate the origin to that point, substitute y = m x and equate the coefficient of x to zero; then c = y' − m x'. The text emphasizes that this operation corresponds to differentiation in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two surfaces of second order through same eight points share intersection curve by linear combination
rubrics_metrics.description: If u=0 and u'=0 are equations of two surfaces of second order passing through the same eight points, then for arbitrary λ, the surface u + λ u' = 0 passes through the same points and thus contains the curve of intersection of the two surfaces; i.e., any linear combination yields another surface sharing the intersection curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a constructive way to generate the family of second-order surfaces through the same eight points and proves that the curve of intersection is contained in every member u+λu'=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: If multiple second-order surfaces intersect in a plane curve, their second intersection is also a plane curve
rubrics_metrics.description: If any number of surfaces of the second order intersect in a plane curve, then any second intersection of those surfaces (if it exists) is also a plane curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manuscript shows this by substituting z=0 (plane of intersection) and comparing coefficients, deducing identities between coefficients of surface equations that force the second intersection to be planar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coefficient-identification when surfaces intersect in plane of xy
rubrics_metrics.description: When two second-order surfaces intersect in the plane z=0, equating the plane polynomial coefficients yields relationships like b=b', c=c', d=d', h=h', k=k' etc., which then lead to linear equations for the line(s) of intersection and show that secondary intersections are planar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coefficient matching after setting z=0 to derive constraints on coefficients; the text explicitly lists these equalities and the derived line equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus of centres of all second-order surfaces through same eight points: intersection of two hyperboloids
rubrics_metrics.description: For the family of second-order surfaces passing through the same eight points, the coordinates of their centres satisfy equations which (after elimination) are equations of two hyperboloids of one sheet; hence the locus of centres is the intersection of those two hyperboloids (a curve).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive centre coordinates via partial differentiation or transformations, eliminate λ, and show the locus equations factor into two hyperboloidal equations; special cases (spheres) yield straight-line loci (corollaries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries for similar surfaces and spheres intersecting same circle
rubrics_metrics.description: If surfaces are similar, the centres of all similar second-order surfaces that have the same curve of intersection lie on the same straight line. In particular, if any number of spheres intersect in the same circle, their centres will be collinear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the general locus result to the special case of similar surfaces or spheres; the text states these as explicit corollaries derived from the general elimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane (2D) analogue: locus of centres for conics through four points is a conic
rubrics_metrics.description: For two plane conics passing through the same four points, any linear combination yields a third conic. The coordinates of the centre of that family satisfy a second-order curve equation; in symmetric cases this locus is a hyperbola through the origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the centre equations, eliminate λ, and recognize the resulting locus as a conic; the text gives special-case simplifications when coefficients are equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus of diameters conjugate to a given plane is a hyperboloid
rubrics_metrics.description: The locus of diameters conjugate to a given plane, in respect of all surfaces of the second order that pass through eight points in space, is the hyperboloid of one sheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate the conjugacy equations, eliminate the multiplier λ, and derive the hyperboloid equation; the manuscript provides the determinant-like coefficient forms leading to that conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of second-order surfaces through tetrahedron faces and edges
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the four face equations t1,t2,t3,t4 of a tetrahedron, surfaces expressed by combinations like t1 t2 + m t1 t3 + n t1 t4 + p t2 t3 = 0 represent all second-order surfaces containing specified pairs of edges (e.g., AC, BD), depending on which combination is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use products and linear combinations of face equations to produce surfaces passing through selected edges and points; the text enumerates particular forms and the sets of lines they contain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surfaces touching two planes along common intersection lines (rectilinear plane contact)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an equation has the form Vi Vj = (linear expression), then when two of the planes coincide, the resulting surface has rectilinear plane contact with the other two planes along the straight lines given by their intersections; the plane containing the two lines of contact is the 'plane of contact.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the degenerate case (two plane factors equal) and rewrite to show contact along lines; the plane of contact passes through the two contact lines and may be used in subsequent incidence theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: If two surfaces have rectilinear plane contact with same two planes, the intersection is two planes forming harmonic radial system
rubrics_metrics.description: If each of two surfaces of second degree has rectilinear plane contact with two given planes, then the surfaces cut each other on two planes which pass through the intersection of the planes of contact and form with those planes a system of four harmonic radial planes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtract surface equations to obtain the plane equations of intersection; these planes pass through the intersection of the contact planes and form the harmonic system as shown in the algebraic manipulation in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation of hyperboloid of one sheet by a line moving on three non-coplanar directrices
rubrics_metrics.description: Given three straight lines no two coplanar, a line moving touching each of the three (one position touches each) generates a ruled surface: the hyperboloid of one sheet; properties include uniqueness of generatrix through each point, directrices lying on the surface, and no two generatrices being coplanar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manuscript gives a geometric genesis: for each point on one directrix there is a unique line touching the other two directrices; these moving lines sweep a non-self-intersecting ruled surface. Degenerate cases (two directrices parallel or meeting) reduce the surface to a plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twisted quadrilateral segment relation on hyperboloid generatrices
rubrics_metrics.description: For three directrices AB, CD, EF and generatrix positions AE, BF, GE, there is a proportionality relation among segments of the twisted quadrilateral ABFE: AC·DF : CE·BD :: AG·KF : GB·EK (a cross-ratio style relation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plane intersections and Hutton's preparatory results to derive the proportional relations among segments when analyzing generatrix placements; the text sketches the proof via plane-triangle decomposition.
